label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Nana,

I wish I were sitting in the kitchen with you tonight. I wish I could have a cup of tea and help with whatever still needs doing, even if helping mostly meant moving something to the wrong place and having you tell me where it actually goes. I’m glad Denise is there. I’ve asked her to read this because I wanted to say more than I can usually manage on the phone, and because every time I’ve tried to write it this week, I’ve got a few sentences in and had to stop.

There’s a lot I want to say about that house. But first, I want to say that I’m excited for you.

Elmwood Terrace looks lovely, Nana. I like that you’ll have that big maple outside your window. The parking lot might not have been the main selling point, but at least you’ll be able to keep an eye on who’s coming and going. And I hear there’s a crib league, which is excellent news for you and potentially quite bad news for everyone currently enjoying a respectable standing in it.

I’m proud of you for choosing this. You looked at what you wanted and made the decision yourself. Nobody made it for you. That doesn’t mean leaving Kathleen Street is easy, or that you have to be cheerful about every bit of it. Fifty-one years is a long time. You’re allowed to be excited about tomorrow and still have a cry in the kitchen tonight. I’m doing something similar from Toronto, except I’ve got a laptop instead of Denise.

I’m sorry I can’t be there for the move. I’m primary on call all week, and I couldn’t find anyone to swap with me. I know you know that. I know you’re not sitting there keeping track of who carried how many boxes, and I know you wouldn’t want me tying myself in knots over it. But I wanted to be there, and it’s hard not to be.

You don’t need to make me feel better about that. I just want you to know that being away isn’t the same as not thinking about it. I’m thinking about you a lot.

When I think about summers at your house, I always end up in the kitchen. I can picture that little television and remember watching the Expos or the Jays while I dried the dishes. I thought being allowed to stay up was such a privilege. Looking back, you’d worked out how to get the dishes dried by a child who thought they were getting away with something. That was a very good arrangement, mostly for you.

But I loved it. I loved being up with you, doing an ordinary thing at a time when I’d normally have been sent to bed. I couldn’t tell you the scores of those games now. I remember being there beside you.

And I remember the back steps early in the morning. You with your tea at six, and me coming out to sit with you. No talking until the cup was done. I didn’t have to tell you anything interesting or answer a lot of questions. I could just sit there. I think about that more often than you probably realise. Life is noisy now, and there’s nearly always something asking for my attention. Those mornings were so quiet. I’m glad we had them.

Of course, you weren’t quite so peaceful when there was a crib board between us.

You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not once. Some grandmothers might have given a small child a little confidence boost. You apparently felt that a small child needed to learn to count properly and accept defeat.

When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still think that was one of my greatest achievements. I’ve had things happen in my career that were considerably harder to explain and nowhere near as rewarding.

I’m so glad you taught me. You gave us something we can still sit down and do together all these years later. We don’t need an occasion or a big plan. We just need the board, a deck of cards, and enough time for you to point out whatever I’ve missed.

That’s why I asked for the crib board. I want to keep using it. I want more games with you.

There are so many little things you’ve done that have stayed with me. When I got the job in Toronto and you sent me that card with a twenty-dollar bill taped inside, saying, “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I was starting this grown-up job, trying to seem like I knew what I was doing, and you were making sure I had dinner. I loved that. I still do.

And last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner and you asked whether the internet was broken again, and whether I’d fixed it. Now every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?”

Honestly, that’s a fairly good summary of my job. People in Toronto use a lot more words to ask me essentially the same thing.

What I love is that you ask. You want to know how my day went, even when my work is a strange thing that interrupts Christmas dinner. You’ve always found your way into whatever was happening in my life. Sometimes with a question, sometimes with pizza money, sometimes by letting me dry dishes for much longer than was strictly necessary so I could see more of the game.

You raised half our family in that kitchen. So much happened there that it’s hard for me to think of the house separately from you. When I picture it, you’re there. Grandpa Walt is part of those memories too, and I’ll be thinking about him this weekend. I wish he could be sitting with us for all of this.

I’m going to miss the house. I don’t want to pretend I won’t, or tell you it’s only a building when we both know how much life happened inside it. I’m grateful I got to be a kid there. I’m grateful that, even after I grew up and moved away, I could still come back to it.

But I don’t want this letter to sound as though all our good times are behind us. They aren’t. I want to hear what you think of Elmwood once you’re properly settled in. I want to hear who you meet, how the crib league goes, and whether anyone there is brave enough to play you twice. I want to sit in your room and look out at the maple and have you tell me things I’ve missed.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I’m glad those things are staying in the family. There will be familiar things in different places. It might feel strange for a while. You don’t have to decide straight away how you feel about all of it.

For tonight, I hope you and Denise get to sit for a bit after the work is done. Have your tea. Talk about whatever you feel like talking about. I wish I were in the chair beside you, but please know how much I love you, and how happy I am that you’ve found somewhere you’re looking forward to living.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, once this rotation is done. We’ll have our first game at the new place, with the crib board between us, and you can show me everything.

And don’t start letting me win now. I’d know something was wrong.

I love you, Nana. See you on December 5. Deal me in.
